sermon:
## The Cross That Empties Every Boast
*Why God chose a crucified Messiah to shame the wise*

**Text:** 1 Corinthians 1:1–2:5 · **Supporting:** Isaiah 29:14; Jeremiah 9:23–24; 1 Corinthians 2:2; Galatians 6:14

A church can be gifted, growing, and dying at the same time. Corinth was. They had eloquence, knowledge, every spiritual gift, and they were tearing themselves apart over which preacher they liked best. Paul does not begin where they expected. He does not flatter their gifts. He goes to the cross and stays there.

**They were measuring the gospel by the wrong ruler**

The fracture looks like loyalty. "I follow Paul," "I follow Apollos," "I follow Cephas," "I follow Christ" (1 Corinthians 1:12). It sounds like devotion. It is competition wearing devotion's clothes. Paul names what is underneath: "For Christ did not send me to baptize but to preach the gospel, and not with words of eloquent wisdom, lest the cross of Christ be emptied of its power" (1 Corinthians 1:17). That phrase — emptied of its power — is the whole letter in five words. They had taken a message that runs entirely on the strength of a dead and risen Christ and started grading it like a rhetoric contest. They preferred the speaker with the better cadence. They were ranking servants the way a city ranks orators.

And a ranked gospel is a domesticated gospel. The moment the message has to survive the same panel that judges a lecturer, it has to dress itself up to compete — and the cross does not dress up. It is the one thing in the world that gets uglier the harder you try to make it impressive. A crucified Messiah cannot be sold as the winning side. So a church that needs its gospel to look like a winner will, slowly and without noticing, stop preaching the cross and start preaching the eloquence around it. That is the quiet death Paul is racing to prevent.

Paul saw the engine. The Corinthians loved teachers the way the world loves winners, and a church that ranks its teachers will eventually rank its Lord.

**God chose the foolish thing on purpose**

Then comes the line that should have stopped them cold: "For the word of the cross is folly to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God" (1 Corinthians 1:18). God did not stumble into an embarrassing method. He selected it. Paul reaches back to Isaiah — "I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the discernment of the discerning I will thwart" (Isaiah 29:14) — to show this is ancient strategy, not first-century accident. The God who confounded Egypt's magicians and Babylon's astrologers chose, at the center of history, the most humiliating instrument the Roman Empire owned. A cross was a slave's death, a public obscenity, a thing you did not say at dinner.

And He picked it. "For the foolishness of God is wiser than men, and the weakness of God is stronger than men" (1 Corinthians 1:25).

Look at who He called, Paul says: "Not many of you were wise according to worldly standards, not many were powerful, not many were of noble birth" (1 Corinthians 1:26). God assembled a church out of the people the world overlooked, "so that no human being might boast in the presence of God" (1 Corinthians 1:29). That is the verb the whole passage circles. Boast. The cross is not merely how we are saved. It is the death of the thing in us that needs to be impressive.

Paul will not even exempt his own preaching. "I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ and him crucified" (1 Corinthians 2:2). He came "in weakness and in fear and much trembling" (1 Corinthians 2:3), refusing the polished delivery they craved, "so that your faith might not rest in the wisdom of men but in the power of God" (1 Corinthians 2:5). He removed the very thing they were grading, on purpose, so they would have nothing to lean on but the crucified Christ.

**The boast we never actually surrendered**

Here is where I have to stop pointing at Corinth, because I know this church too well, and I know my own heart in it. We do not split over Apollos and Cephas. We split over worship styles and personalities and the preacher who finally said it the way we always wanted it said. We rank our teachers. We have our man. And underneath the loyalty is the same machinery — a hunger to be on the side that looks wise, to belong to the impressive thing. I have preached sermons more concerned that the room admire the argument than that the room meet the Christ. That is eloquence emptying the cross of its power, and I have done it from a pulpit.

The Corinthians were not pagans. They were Christians who had carried the world's scoreboard into the sanctuary and kept score with it. So have we.

But the cross will not be graded. It can only be received. Jeremiah names the only boast left standing: "Let not the wise man boast in his wisdom… but let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows me" (Jeremiah 9:23–24). And Paul, writing to these same competitive Corinthians later, lands the whole matter: "far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ" (Galatians 6:14).

Christ crucified is the wisdom of God precisely where the world reads only failure. The strong are shamed not by a stronger strong man but by a bleeding one. The boast is not lowered. It is killed and buried with Him, and what rises has nothing left to prove.

So bring your scoreboard to the foot of the cross. Set it down. It does not work there. The crucified Christ did not come to win your argument. He came to end your need to win.

The cross ends our boasting.

## Infants Fighting Over Field Hands
*The wise discovered they were toddlers, and the building was holy ground*

**Text:** 1 Corinthians 2:6–3:23 · **Supporting:** Isaiah 64:4; 1 Corinthians 3:9; 1 Corinthians 3:16–17; Ephesians 2:21–22

The people most certain of their maturity are often the ones quarreling in the nursery. Corinth prided itself on wisdom. Paul looks at the same church and sees infants. Both things were true at once, and that is the unsettling part.

**There is a wisdom they could not access by being clever**

Paul begins by granting them something. "Yet among the mature we do impart wisdom" (1 Corinthians 2:6). There is a deeper wisdom — but it is not the wisdom they were chasing. It is "a secret and hidden wisdom of God, which God decreed before the ages for our glory" (1 Corinthians 2:7), the wisdom the rulers of this age missed so completely that "they crucified the Lord of glory" (1 Corinthians 2:8). The smartest men in the room executed God. Quoting Isaiah, Paul says, "What no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor the heart of man imagined, what God has prepared for those who love him" (1 Corinthians 2:9; Isaiah 64:4). This is not knowledge you climb to. It is knowledge revealed by the Spirit, "for the Spirit searches everything, even the depths of God" (1 Corinthians 2:10).

The Corinthians thought spiritual maturity was a higher IQ. Paul says it is the Spirit's gift, given to those the world calls foolish. Their pride in wisdom was the very evidence they had missed it.

**Their fighting exposed them**

Then the blow. "But I, brothers, could not address you as spiritual people, but as people of the flesh, as infants in Christ" (1 Corinthians 3:1). He fed them milk because they could not take solid food — and the proof was not their theology exam. It was their behavior. "For while there is jealousy and strife among you, are you not of the flesh?" (1 Corinthians 3:3). The Corinthians measured maturity by how much they knew. Paul measured it by how they treated each other. By his ruler, a church that fights over teachers is a church of toddlers, however much it knows.

And the teachers they were fighting over? Paul demolishes the pedestal. "What then is Apollos? What is Paul? Servants through whom you believed… I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth" (1 Corinthians 3:5–6). Field hands. Day laborers in someone else's vineyard. "So neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but only God who gives the growth" (1 Corinthians 3:7). You cannot build a faction around a field hand. The Corinthians had inflated servants into celebrities and then divided over the celebrities they had invented.

There is a freedom in that demotion the Corinthians could not feel because they were too busy ranking. Pride always wants a champion to attach itself to, because the champion's status becomes the follower's status, and the followers were really boasting in themselves through the men they claimed. If Apollos is a field hand and Paul is a field hand, then the church does not belong to either of them — it belongs to the One who owns the field. The growth was never theirs to give. "Each will receive his wages according to his labor" (1 Corinthians 3:8), and not one of them can take credit for the harvest. The teacher you idolized and the teacher you despised are doing the same humble work for the same Lord. You have nothing to divide over, because the men you were dividing over do not even own the thing you were claiming.

**You are God's temple, and that changes the fight**

Then Paul lifts the image off the farm and onto holy ground. "You are God's field, God's building" (1 Corinthians 3:9). And he presses it until it becomes a warning that should make every church tremble: "Do you not know that you are God's temple and that God's Spirit dwells in you? If anyone destroys God's temple, God will destroy him. For God's temple is holy, and you are that temple" (1 Corinthians 3:16–17).

Read that slowly, because the Corinthians clearly had not. The temple in view is not the individual believer here — it is the church, the gathered body, the people. Their squabbling was not a personality clash. It was vandalism of a sanctuary. Every faction was taking a hammer to holy ground. Paul tells the Ephesians the same building "grows into a holy temple in the Lord… a dwelling place for God by the Spirit" (Ephesians 2:21–22). The place where God now lives is not made of stone. It is made of the people you are tempted to divide from.

Here is where I stop and include myself, because I have been a hammer in the wall of the temple I was called to build. I have let a disagreement curdle into a faction. I have nursed the quiet satisfaction of being right while the body I serve thinned out around me. We treat the church like a coalition to be won, an argument to be settled, a side to be taken. Paul says it is holy ground, and the Spirit is in it, and you are swinging at God.

So Paul ends with a strange freedom. "So let no one boast in men. For all things are yours, whether Paul or Apollos or Cephas… all are yours, and you are Christ's, and Christ is God's" (1 Corinthians 3:21–23). Stop claiming a teacher as your trophy — they all belong to you, every one, given by the God who owns the whole field. You do not need a faction. You have a Father, and the building He raised was paid for at the cross and filled by His Spirit. That is the only foundation, "for no one can lay a foundation other than that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ" (1 Corinthians 3:11).

You do not defend the temple by winning. You stop swinging.

You are God's temple, not factions.

## Already Rich, Already Reigning, Already Wrong
*A church drunk on borrowed gifts meets apostles counted as the world's garbage*

**Text:** 1 Corinthians 4:1–21 · **Supporting:** 1 Corinthians 4:7; 1 Corinthians 4:20; Romans 12:3; 2 Corinthians 4:7

There is a particular kind of pride that only grace can produce. It is the pride of a person who has been given everything and begins to carry it like an achievement. Corinth had it. They were rich, they were reigning, they were full — and they had forgotten that every ounce of it arrived as a gift.

**Servants are judged by one Master, not by the room**

Paul starts by reframing how a leader should be regarded. "This is how one should regard us, as servants of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God" (1 Corinthians 4:1). A steward's job is faithfulness, not applause: "it is required of stewards that they be found trustworthy" (1 Corinthians 4:2). Then he loosens the Corinthians' grip on the gavel they had grabbed. "But with me it is a very small thing that I should be judged by you or by any human court… It is the Lord who judges me" (1 Corinthians 4:3–4).

The Corinthians had appointed themselves a panel, ranking apostles like contestants. Paul declines to appear before their court. He is not unaccountable — he is accountable to Someone they cannot impersonate. "Therefore do not pronounce judgment before the time, before the Lord comes" (1 Corinthians 4:5). The church that loves to rank its teachers has confused itself with the judgment seat.

**The question that dismantles every boast**

Then comes the sentence that should be carved over the door of every gifted church. "For who sees anything different in you? What do you have that you did not receive? If then you received it, why do you boast as if you did not receive it?" (1 Corinthians 4:7).

Sit in front of that question. Everything they were proud of — their knowledge, their eloquence, their gifts, their faith itself — had been handed to them. Not earned. Received. And the moment you boast in a gift as if it were an achievement, you have insulted the Giver and lied about yourself. Paul is not asking them to be modest. He is asking them to be accurate. A church congratulating itself on grace has misunderstood the word.

Then the irony turns to a blade. "Already you have all you want! Already you have become rich! Without us you have become kings!" (1 Corinthians 4:8). They thought the kingdom had fully arrived and they were already on thrones — comfortable, satisfied, reigning. Paul answers with a portrait that should have emptied the room. "For I think that God has exhibited us apostles as last of all, like men sentenced to death… We are fools for Christ's sake… We are weak… we are held in disrepute. To the present hour we hunger and thirst, we are poorly dressed and buffeted and homeless" (1 Corinthians 4:9–11). And then the word that lands like spit: "we have become, and are still, like the scum of the world, the refuse of all things" (1 Corinthians 4:13).

Garbage. The apostles, while the Corinthians played at being kings, were the world's trash. The contrast is not accidental. The kingdom of God advances through people the empire throws away — and the church basking in comfort had mistaken its borrowed glory for arrival.

This is the pattern that runs through the whole Bible and the whole letter: God works through weakness so the glory cannot be confused for ours. The Corinthians had collapsed the timeline — they thought the reigning had already started, that the suffering was behind them, that they had graduated past the cross into the crown. But there is no graduating past the cross in this age. The apostles, beaten and homeless and counted as refuse, were not failing at the Christian life. They were living it. The comfort the Corinthians mistook for maturity was the very thing exposing how little they understood the kingdom they claimed to rule.

And the test still holds. A church grown comfortable, certain it has arrived, proud of what it has built, should read the apostles' resume — beaten, homeless, counted as garbage — and ask why its own life looks so little like the lives of the men who carried the gospel to it. The power Paul means is not the power of a full building and a smooth program. It is the power that looks, to the watching world, like weakness, because it is the power of a crucified Lord at work in people the world overlooks.

**The kingdom is power, not talk**

Here is the verdict that lands the whole chapter: "For the kingdom of God does not consist in talk but in power" (1 Corinthians 4:20). Corinth had endless talk. Eloquence to spare. What they lacked was the cruciform power that looks, from the outside, exactly like weakness.

I cannot read this and stay outside it. I have stood in pulpits well-fed and well-dressed and quietly proud of a gift I did not give myself. I have boasted as if I did not receive it. The question — what do you have that you did not receive — undoes me, because the honest answer is nothing. Not my mind, not my call, not my faith, not the breath I am using right now. A pastor congratulating himself on grace is the Corinthian disease in a collar, and I have carried it.

Paul ends not with a lecture but a father's heart. "I do not write these things to make you ashamed, but to admonish you as my beloved children" (1 Corinthians 4:14). This is grief, not contempt. He has "this treasure in jars of clay, to show that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us" (2 Corinthians 4:7). And the treasure is Christ — the King who became refuse, sentenced to death outside the city, last of all, so that beggars like us could be made rich. The cross is the pattern. The crucified Christ did not reign by climbing. He reigned by being thrown away. And everything you have, you have because He was.

So count it again. All of it received. Then there is nothing left to crown but Him.

Boast in nothing you received as gift.

## Leaven, Lawsuits, and a Body You No Longer Own
*A tolerant church discovers that grace is not a license and the body is not disposable*

**Text:** 1 Corinthians 5:1–6:20 · **Supporting:** 1 Corinthians 5:6–7; Deuteronomy 17:7; 1 Corinthians 6:11; 1 Corinthians 6:19–20

There is a tolerance that is really cowardice, and a tolerance that is really pride, and Corinth had both. They were boasting about their openness while a sin sat in the middle of the congregation that even the pagans around them would not stomach. Paul does not admire their broadmindedness. He grieves it.

**The leaven they were proud of**

"It is actually reported that there is sexual immorality among you, and of a kind that is not tolerated even among pagans, for a man has his father's wife" (1 Corinthians 5:1). Then the line that exposes the whole posture: "And you are arrogant! Ought you not rather to mourn?" (1 Corinthians 5:2). They had turned a blind eye and called it grace. They were swollen with pride over their tolerance while the body rotted.

Paul reaches for an image from the Passover kitchen. "Your boasting is not good. Do you not know that a little leaven leavens the whole lump? Cleanse out the old leaven that you may be a new lump, as you really are unleavened. For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed" (1 Corinthians 5:6–7). Sin in the church is not a private matter quarantined in one corner. It works through the whole loaf. And the standard he invokes is ancient — "Purge the evil person from among you" (1 Corinthians 5:13), the very words Moses gave Israel (Deuteronomy 17:7). This is not cruelty. It is love refusing to watch a man and a church destroy themselves and call it acceptance.

We have been trained to think the loving thing is always the soft thing, that confrontation is the opposite of grace. Paul refuses the trade. The whole point of removing the man was redemptive — "that his spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord" (1 Corinthians 5:5). This is surgery, not execution. The cancer is cut out so the body lives and so the patient himself might be healed. A church too cowardly to confront sin is not more loving than a church willing to. It is only more comfortable, and comfort that watches a brother die in his sin is not love at all. It is indifference wearing love's name.

The same Christ our Passover lamb who was sacrificed to cleanse the leaven is the One whose blood now bought the body Corinth was treating as disposable. The cross does both things at once — it purges and it purchases. It will not leave the sin in the loaf, and it will not let the body be thrown away. To take grace seriously is to take both seriously, the holiness that cuts and the love that buys, because they met in the same blood.

The Corinthians thought judging sin was harsh and tolerating it was loving. Paul reverses it. The harsh thing was leaving the man in his sin to be ruined. The loving thing was to act.

**Dragging brothers before pagan judges**

Then Paul turns to the courtroom. "When one of you has a grievance against another, does he dare go to law before the unrighteous instead of the saints?" (1 Corinthians 6:1). The same church too soft to confront real sin was hard enough to sue a brother in front of the city. "To have lawsuits at all with one another is already a defeat for you. Why not rather suffer wrong? Why not rather be defrauded?" (1 Corinthians 6:7).

There it is. The kingdom logic that the world cannot compute. The point is not winning the case. The point is whether you would rather be wronged than disgrace the gospel before the watching pagans. A people who will one day judge angels (1 Corinthians 6:3) were running to pagan magistrates to settle a quarrel over money. Their priorities were inverted. They confronted the wrong things and tolerated the wrong things, every time.

**The body you were bought to honor**

Then Paul names the lie underneath it all — a slogan the Corinthians were repeating: "All things are lawful for me" (1 Corinthians 6:12). They had taken Christian freedom and twisted it into permission to use the body however they pleased, including with prostitutes (1 Corinthians 6:15–16). Paul answers with ownership. "Do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God? You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body" (1 Corinthians 6:19–20).

You are not your own. The body is not disposable, not neutral, not yours to spend. It was purchased — at the cross, with blood, by Christ our Passover lamb who was sacrificed so the leaven could be cleansed out. The crucified Christ did not buy your soul and leave your body in the gutter. He bought all of you. The price tag is the cross.

And here is the mercy buried in the middle of this hard chapter, easy to miss because it arrives like a thunderclap: "And such were some of you. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God" (1 Corinthians 6:11). Such were some of you. Past tense. The list of sins that bars people from the kingdom — Paul read it over the very people now seated in the church, and then said: that is who you were, not who you are.

I cannot stand over this congregation as a man who got it right. I have been arrogant where I should have mourned. I have tolerated in myself the thing I would confront in another, and dressed my cowardice up as grace, and sued the world's way in my heart for grievances I should have absorbed. The leaven is not only out there. It is in me. And the same blood that bought my body confronts the way I have spent it.

So hear it as both warning and rescue. You are not your own. The One who owns you bled for you. Honor Him with the body He paid for.

You were bought; honor God bodily.

## Called Where Grace Found You
*Neither the ascetic nor the libertine — undivided devotion in the life you already have*

**Text:** 1 Corinthians 7:1–40 · **Supporting:** 1 Corinthians 7:17; 1 Corinthians 7:23; 1 Corinthians 7:35; Matthew 6:33

Every age has its two errors about the body, and they always travel together. One says the body is dirty, so marriage is a compromise and sex is beneath the truly spiritual. The other says the body is everything, so restraint is repression and freedom means doing whatever you want. Corinth had both, sitting in the same pews, sending Paul their questions. He refuses both.

**Marriage is not a concession to weakness**

Some in Corinth had taken the high spiritual road: "It is good for a man not to have sexual relations with a woman" (1 Corinthians 7:1) — a slogan they were quoting, possibly even to justify withholding from their spouses. Paul answers with a startling mutuality. "The husband should give to his wife her conjugal rights, and likewise the wife to her husband. For the wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does. Likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does" (1 Corinthians 7:3–4). In a Roman world where a husband owned everything, Paul hands each spouse authority over the other — a mutual self-giving that the ascetics, with all their spiritual pride, had never imagined.

He will not let them despise marriage as second-class. Marriage is a calling, not a failure of nerve. The ascetic who looks down on the married believer has not climbed higher. He has missed the point.

**Singleness is not a tragedy to be fixed**

Then Paul turns the other way, toward the libertine instinct and toward a church that pitied the unmarried. He commends singleness with a freedom the world finds incomprehensible. "I wish that all were as I myself am" (1 Corinthians 7:7) — single, undistracted, free for the Lord. "The unmarried man is anxious about the things of the Lord, how to please the Lord… I say this for your own benefit… to promote good order and to secure your undivided devotion to the Lord" (1 Corinthians 7:32, 35).

There is the phrase the whole chapter is bending toward. Undivided devotion. Not a rule about who may marry. A center of gravity. Paul is not anti-marriage or pro-marriage. He is pro-Christ, and he is asking one question of every situation: how is your heart most undividedly His?

The ascetics and the libertines look like opposites, but they share one root: both think the gospel is mainly about the body's appetites, one by suppressing them and one by indulging them. Paul will not let either be the center. The center is the Lord, and the body — married or single, fed or fasting — is meant to serve Him. That is why he can hold marriage and singleness side by side without ranking them. The married believer is not less devoted and the single believer is not less complete. The question is never the circumstance. The question is whether, in that circumstance, the heart is undivided. Corinth wanted a hierarchy of holiness. Paul gave them a single Lord over every station.

So Paul can say, almost in passing, "the appointed time has grown very short" (1 Corinthians 7:29) — live as those whose hope is fixed past this passing world. The single life and the married life are both short, both temporary, both swallowed up in the coming of Christ. That is not a reason to despise either. It is a reason to hold both loosely and to hold the Lord tightly, because the situation will pass and He will not.

**Stay where you were called, and be His there**

So Paul lands on a principle he repeats three times, because the Corinthians kept thinking the answer was to change their circumstances. "Only let each person lead the life that the Lord has assigned to him, and to which God has called him… let each one remain in the condition in which he was called" (1 Corinthians 7:17, 20). Married, single, slave, free, Jew, Greek — grace found you somewhere, and that somewhere is where you live for the Lord now. You do not need a different life to be devoted. You need to be devoted in the one you have.

And underneath it, the same purchase that runs through this whole letter: "You were bought with a price; do not become slaves of men" (1 Corinthians 7:23). The reason the single believer is free and the married believer is free and the slave is the Lord's freedman is that Christ paid for all of them at the cross. The crucified Christ did not redeem you into a holding pattern, waiting for the right circumstances to begin obeying. He redeemed you into the kitchen and the cubicle and the marriage and the loneliness you are sitting in right now.

I have to confess the lie I have believed most often is the one Paul is dismantling: that real devotion begins after the circumstances change. After the marriage is healed. After the season passes. After the loneliness lifts. I have treated my actual life as the waiting room for the spiritual life. Paul says the actual life is the spiritual life. Where grace found you is where you are called. There is no other location.

The Corinthians wanted a rule that would settle every case. Paul gives them a Lord instead, and one undivided aim that reorganizes every case: "Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness" (Matthew 6:33). Married, you seek it together. Single, you seek it free. The situation is not the calling. Christ is the calling, in the situation. The waiting room was never real. The kingdom does not begin when your circumstances improve; it began the day grace found you, in the place it found you, and it is asking for your undivided heart there.

So stop waiting for a different life to start living for Him. He bought the one you have.

Live for the Lord, undivided.

## Knowledge Puffs Up, Love Builds Up
*When being right wounds the weak, and an apostle lays down his rights*

**Text:** 1 Corinthians 8:1–9:27 · **Supporting:** 1 Corinthians 8:1; 1 Corinthians 9:19; 1 Corinthians 9:22; Romans 14:15

You can be entirely correct and entirely wrong at the same time. The Corinthians proved it. They had their theology right about idols — and they were using that correct theology to wound the people Christ died for. Paul does not argue with their doctrine. He argues with what their doctrine had done to their love.

**Right answer, ruined brother**

The question was meat sacrificed to idols. The mature Corinthians had it figured out: an idol is nothing, there is one God, so the meat is just meat. They were not wrong. And Paul grants it fully. "We know that 'an idol has no real existence,' and that 'there is no God but one'" (1 Corinthians 8:4). But before he agrees with their theology, he plants a warning over the whole conversation. "This 'knowledge' puffs up, but love builds up. If anyone imagines that he knows something, he does not yet know as he ought to know" (1 Corinthians 8:1–2).

There is the contrast the whole passage runs on. Knowledge inflates. Love constructs. And a man who is proud of his knowledge has already demonstrated he does not yet truly know — because the highest knowledge produces love, not a swollen head.

There is a kind of knowing that puffs and a kind that bows, and you can tell them apart by what they do to the people around you. The knowledge that puffs makes you taller and the room smaller. The knowledge that builds makes you a servant of the weakest conscience in the room. The Corinthians had the facts and missed the point so completely that their correct theology became a weapon against the very people Christ died for. To know God truly is to start loving what He loves, and He loves the weak brother more than He loves your right to be right about the meat.

That is why Paul ends with an athlete who will not be disqualified — because love of the weak is not a feeling that visits you, it is a discipline you train into your body day after day. The flesh asserts itself by reflex. Love lays itself down by practice. A Christian who never trains in surrender will assert his rights every time it costs him something, and call it conviction.

The danger was not the meat. It was the weaker believer watching. "But take care that this right of yours does not somehow become a stumbling block to the weak" (1 Corinthians 8:9). A brother with a tender conscience, newly out of paganism, sees the mature Christian eating in the idol's temple and is dragged back toward the worship he just escaped. "And so by your knowledge this weak person is destroyed, the brother for whom Christ died" (1 Corinthians 8:11). Then the sentence that should end every argument we win at someone's expense: "Thus, sinning against your brothers and wounding their conscience when it is weak, you sin against Christ" (1 Corinthians 8:12).

You were right about the meat. You were wrong about your brother. And being right about the meat did not make you innocent. It made the wound worse.

**The apostle who surrendered his own rights**

Then Paul does the most disarming thing in the letter. Instead of telling them to give up their freedom, he shows them his own back, scarred from a lifetime of giving up his. Chapter 9 is one long demonstration. He had every right to be paid for his ministry — he proves it from the law, from the temple, from the words of Jesus (1 Corinthians 9:7–14). And then: "But I have made no use of any of these rights" (1 Corinthians 9:15). He worked with his hands rather than burden them, "that in my preaching I may present the gospel free of charge, so as not to make full use of my right in the gospel" (1 Corinthians 9:18).

Why? "For though I am free from all, I have made myself a servant to all, that I might win more of them" (1 Corinthians 9:19). And then the famous summary of a surrendered life: "I have become all things to all people, that by all means I might save some" (1 Corinthians 9:22). The apostle who could have stood on his rights chose to die to them, repeatedly, so that nothing about him would get between a weak person and the gospel.

The Corinthians asked, can I exercise my right? Paul answered with a man who spent his whole ministry refusing his.

**The cross is the pattern, and the discipline is real**

Paul ends with an athlete in training. "Every athlete exercises self-control in all things… I discipline my body and keep it under control, lest after preaching to others I myself should be disqualified" (1 Corinthians 9:25, 27). Love that builds the brother is not soft sentiment. It is disciplined surrender, the daily death of self-assertion.

And the model under all of it is the crucified Christ. Romans says it plainly: "By what you eat, do not destroy the one for whom Christ died" (Romans 14:15). The whole argument is cruciform. Christ had every right — the rights of God Himself — and laid them down, all of them, to the point of a cross, for people who were nothing but weak. The mature Corinthian, clutching his correct theology and his Christian freedom, was standing in exactly the opposite posture from his Savior.

I know this sin from the inside, because the temptation to win is strongest when I am right. I have been theologically correct and pastorally cruel in the same sentence. I have used a true thing to wound a tender person and walked away satisfied that I held the better argument. That is knowledge puffing up while a brother Christ died for is left bleeding on the floor of my certainty. Being right has never once made me Christlike. Only laying it down has.

So the question is not whether you are free. You are. The question is whether you love the weak brother enough to act as if you are not.

Surrender your rights for love.

## They Had the Cloud and Still Fell
*Warnings from the wilderness, and freedom bent toward the neighbor's good*

**Text:** 1 Corinthians 10:1–11:1 · **Supporting:** 1 Corinthians 10:12; 1 Corinthians 10:21; 1 Corinthians 10:31; Numbers 14:29–30

Confidence is most dangerous right before the fall. The generation Paul reaches back for had seen more of God's power in a week than most of us see in a lifetime — and their bones bleached the desert floor. He puts that generation in front of the overconfident Corinthians as a mirror, because a church that thinks it cannot fall is the church most likely to.

**Privilege is not protection**

Paul stacks up Israel's advantages like a man laying out evidence. "Our fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea, and all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink… and the Rock was Christ" (1 Corinthians 10:1–4). Every one of them had the sign, the deliverance, the bread, the water, Christ Himself in their midst. And then: "Nevertheless, with most of them God was not pleased, for they were overthrown in the wilderness" (1 Corinthians 10:5).

That generation God swore would not enter the land — "your dead bodies shall fall in this wilderness" (Numbers 14:29). They had the cloud and the sea and the rock, and they still craved evil, still grumbled, still played the harlot, and still fell. Paul drives the point home: "Now these things took place as examples for us… Therefore let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall" (1 Corinthians 10:6, 12).

The Corinthians, proud of their knowledge and their freedom, thought their privileges made them invulnerable. Israel had more privileges and died in the sand. Standing is not a possession you own. It is a grace you depend on, and the man surest he cannot fall has already loosened his grip.

But the warning is not meant to leave you anxious — Paul slips in a promise in the middle of it. "God is faithful, and he will not let you be tempted beyond your ability, but with the temptation he will also provide the way of escape" (1 Corinthians 10:13). The same God who let Israel fall when they presumed will hold up everyone who depends on Him. So the cure for overconfidence is not despair. It is a humility that keeps both eyes on the faithfulness of God instead of the strength of self. The fall comes when you stop watching for the door He always provides, because you were too sure you would never need it.

This is the strange mercy buried in the warning: the safest believer is the one most aware of how easily he could fall. Self-distrust drives him to dependence, and dependence keeps him standing. The Corinthian who said "I would never" was already on the ground. The believer who says "but for grace, I would" is the one grace is holding up.

**Two tables you cannot share**

Then Paul names the line their freedom kept trying to cross. They were rationalizing attendance at idol feasts — the meat is nothing, the idol is nothing, surely it is harmless. Paul answers with the table. "The cup of blessing that we bless, is it not a participation in the blood of Christ? The bread that we break, is it not a participation in the body of Christ?" (1 Corinthians 10:16). Communion is real fellowship — and so is the idol feast, fellowship with demons (1 Corinthians 10:20). "You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons. You cannot partake of the table of the Lord and the table of demons" (1 Corinthians 10:21).

There is no neutral ground here. The Corinthians wanted their freedom to be infinitely elastic, stretching to cover the demonic feast and the Lord's Supper in the same week. Paul says the two tables exclude each other. You belong to one Lord, and that belonging makes some freedoms impossible — not because the meat has power, but because your loyalty is not divisible.

**Bend every freedom toward the other**

And then, having warned them, Paul does not leave them paralyzed by a list of rules. He hands them one governing aim that turns liberty into love. "'All things are lawful,' but not all things are helpful. 'All things are lawful,' but not all things build up. Let no one seek his own good, but the good of his neighbor" (1 Corinthians 10:23–24).

There is the pivot. Freedom is real. But freedom's purpose is not your own comfort — it is the neighbor's good. And the whole thing comes to rest on the largest aim a human life can have: "So, whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God" (1 Corinthians 10:31). Every ordinary act — the meal, the conversation, the freedom exercised or laid down — bent toward God's glory and the neighbor's good.

This is where I am exposed, because I am most likely to fall in the area where I am most confident, and I rarely see it coming. I have stood on a thing I was free to do and never once asked whether it built up the person watching me do it. I have assumed my standing was secure precisely where it was thinnest. Israel is a mirror, and the face in it is mine.

Paul ends with the only safe place to put your confidence: "Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ" (1 Corinthians 11:1). The Rock that followed Israel was Christ — the same Christ who would be struck for them, broken at a table, His body and blood the true food and drink. The cup we bless is His blood; the bread we break is His body. The crucified Christ is the One who poured Himself out entirely for the good of others, and the imitation Paul asks for is cross-shaped: a freedom spent, not hoarded, for the neighbor God put in front of you.

So take heed if you think you stand. And then stop thinking about yourself at all.

Whatever you do, seek another's good.

## A Table That Was Meant to Make Us One
*Worship that dishonors, a Supper that divides, and the body we were despising*

**Text:** 1 Corinthians 11:2–34 · **Supporting:** 1 Corinthians 11:20–22; 1 Corinthians 11:26; 1 Corinthians 11:29; Luke 22:19–20

The most sacred thing in the church can become the place where the church is most ashamed of itself. Corinth managed it. The Lord's Supper — the meal meant to make many into one body — had become the hour their divisions were most visible. They came together and came apart at the same table.

**Their gatherings dishonored both order and one another**

Paul moves into the matter of their worship gatherings, and the problem is not enthusiasm. It is contempt — for order, and for each other. He addresses the conduct of worship first (1 Corinthians 11:2–16), insisting that what happens in the assembly should honor God and reflect the way He made men and women, not erase it in a scramble for self-expression. But the heavier charge comes at the Supper.

"When you come together, it is not the Lord's supper that you eat. For in eating, each one goes ahead with his own meal. One goes hungry, another gets drunk" (1 Corinthians 11:20–21). The wealthy arrived early with their food and feasted; the poor, the slaves who came late from work, the day laborers — they sat with empty hands and watched. Then the line that exposes the wound: "Do you despise the church of God and humiliate those who have nothing? What shall I say to you? Shall I commend you in this? No, I will not" (1 Corinthians 11:22).

The meal that proclaimed one body had become a stage for the social ranking of the city. The rich kept their tables; the poor kept their shame. They were eating the Lord's Supper in a posture that denied everything the Lord's Supper meant.

**Remember whose body this is**

So Paul takes them back to the night it began, handing on the tradition he received. "The Lord Jesus on the night when he was betrayed took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it, and said, 'This is my body, which is for you. Do this in remembrance of me.' In the same way also he took the cup… 'This cup is the new covenant in my blood. Do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of me'" (1 Corinthians 11:23–25; cf. Luke 22:19–20).

This is the body broken for them. This is the blood of the new covenant, poured out for them. And what was the body for? "For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord's death until he comes" (1 Corinthians 11:26). Every time they ate, they preached a sermon — a sermon about a body broken so that the broken could be made one. And they were preaching it while humiliating the very people that body was broken to gather in.

This is the scandal that should reach our own gatherings, because the social ranking did not stay in Corinth. We have our own ways of letting the comfortable feast while the struggling sit at the edge with empty hands — our own quiet sortings of who matters in the room. The Supper was God's standing rebuke to all of it: one loaf, one cup, one body, no head table. When a church lets the world's divisions survive at the Lord's table, it is not adapting communion to reality. It is denying the only reality communion proclaims — that the broken body made enemies into one family, and there are no second-class members of a body bought by one blood.

The Supper is the great leveler precisely because the price was the same for everyone. The rich Corinthian and the slave who came late from work were bought with the identical blood, seated at the identical table, fed with the identical bread. To rank them is to claim the cross cost more for one than the other. It did not. It cost everything, for all of them, equally.

A church gorging itself while the poor go hungry, under the sign of a Savior who gave His body away, is not merely disorganized. It is contradicting the cross with its mouth full.

**Discern the body — both bodies**

Then the warning. "Whoever, therefore, eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord in an unworthy manner will be guilty concerning the body and blood of the Lord" (1 Corinthians 11:27). And the diagnosis: "For anyone who eats and drinks without discerning the body eats and drinks judgment on himself" (1 Corinthians 11:29).

Discern the body. There are two bodies in view and Paul means both. The body and blood of Christ on the table — the crucified Lord proclaimed in the bread. And the body of believers around the table — the poor brother you stepped over to reach your own meal. To despise the second is to fail to discern the first. You cannot honor the broken body of Christ while humiliating the body of Christ that is the church. They are bound together at this table. That was the whole point of the table.

I have to take this one personally, because I have presided at this table and been more careful about the order of the elements than about the souls in the room. I have made the Supper tidy and missed the brother sitting at the edge of it. We can guard the doctrine of communion and still fail the people communion was meant to unite, and I have done both in the same service. To handle the body of the Lord while ignoring the body of the Lord around me is the Corinthian sin in a more respectable coat.

So Paul tells them to examine themselves and to wait for one another (1 Corinthians 11:28, 33). Not so the worthy can come and the unworthy stay home — none of us is worthy, that is the meaning of the cross — but so that the table stops dividing what Christ died to unite. The crucified Christ gave His one body for many. The Supper says so every time. Eat it, then, like people who believe it.

Discern the body at the table.

## The Parts You Were Ready to Cut Off
*One Spirit, many gifts, and no member the body is allowed to discard*

**Text:** 1 Corinthians 12:1–31 · **Supporting:** 1 Corinthians 12:7; 1 Corinthians 12:11; 1 Corinthians 12:21; Romans 12:4–5

A church can take the very gifts meant to bind it together and turn them into a ranking system that tears it apart. Corinth did. They had the gifts. They were competing over them. And Paul has to remind a church drunk on the showy gifts that the Giver had one body in mind, not a leaderboard.

**One Spirit behind all of it**

Paul begins by anchoring every gift to a single source. "Now there are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit; and there are varieties of service, but the same Lord; and there are varieties of activities, but it is the same God who empowers them all in everyone" (1 Corinthians 12:4–6). Same Spirit, same Lord, same God. The variety is real, but the source is one — which means competition over gifts is competition over which expression of the same Spirit is better, an argument that collapses the moment you say it out loud.

Then the purpose, the phrase the whole chapter bends toward: "To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good" (1 Corinthians 12:7). Not for display. Not for status. For the common good. Your gift was never about you. It was given to you for them. And the distribution is not yours to negotiate: "All these are empowered by one and the same Spirit, who apportions to each one individually as he wills" (1 Corinthians 12:11). You did not choose your gift, and you cannot envy your way into another. The Spirit assigned it, deliberately, for the body.

Envy in the body is therefore a quarrel with the Giver, not with the brother. When the foot resents the hand, it is really accusing God of building the body wrong. And the accusation cuts both ways — the impressive part that looks down on the hidden part is just as much in rebellion, because it imagines the Spirit made a mistake in needing the lowly joint at all. Paul closes the door on both. The arrangement is God's, the distribution is God's, the purpose is the common good, and the only fitting response to your gift is to put it to work for the people the Spirit gave it for. Gratitude builds the body. Envy and contempt both tear it down.

The Corinthians treated gifts as personal trophies. Paul says they are tools the Spirit hands out for everyone's good. A gift hoarded for self-promotion has been turned against its own purpose.

**One body, and no part expendable**

Then comes the image Paul refuses to let go of. "For just as the body is one and has many members… so it is with Christ" (1 Corinthians 12:12). He pushes it past the point of comfort. The foot cannot quit because it is not a hand; the ear cannot resign because it is not an eye (1 Corinthians 12:15–16). "If the whole body were an eye, where would be the sense of hearing?" (1 Corinthians 12:17). A body that is all one impressive part is not a body. It is a monstrosity.

And then the sentence aimed straight at the competitive heart of Corinth: "The eye cannot say to the hand, 'I have no need of you,' nor again the head to the feet, 'I have no need of you'" (1 Corinthians 12:21). No member of the body is allowed to discard another. The very thing the Corinthians were doing — ranking some gifts as essential and some believers as unnecessary — Paul declares anatomically impossible and spiritually deadly.

Then he turns it inside out. "On the contrary, the parts of the body that seem to be weaker are indispensable, and on those parts of the body that we think less honorable we bestow the greater honor" (1 Corinthians 12:22–23). God built the body so that the parts we are tempted to overlook are the ones we cannot do without. "But God has so composed the body, giving greater honor to the part that lacked it, that there may be no division in the body, but that the members may have the same care for one another" (1 Corinthians 12:24–25). The whole arrangement is engineered against the very factionalism Corinth loved.

**You are members of one another**

Paul will not let it stay abstract. "Now you are the body of Christ and individually members of it" (1 Corinthians 12:27). Romans says the same: "we, though many, are one body in Christ, and individually members one of another" (Romans 12:4–5). Not members of an organization. Members of one another. When one suffers, all suffer; when one is honored, all rejoice (1 Corinthians 12:26).

I am convicted here as a pastor who has, more than once, quietly valued the visible gifts over the hidden ones — celebrated the platform and overlooked the woman praying at 5 a.m. and the man who sets up chairs no one thanks. I have run a church more like an eye congratulating itself than a body caring for its weakest joint. The temptation to say "I have no need of you" rarely speaks out loud. It just stops looking at the parts that do not impress, and I have stopped looking.

But the body is one because Christ is one, and we were all "baptized into one body" by one Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:13). The crucified Christ gave one body on the cross to make us one body now. The hand you were ready to discard and the eye you envied were both purchased by the same blood and joined by the same Spirit to the same Lord. There is no expendable member at the foot of that cross.

So look again at the part of the body you were ready to do without. The Spirit put it there. On purpose. For you.

The Spirit gifts for one body.

## The More Excellent Way
*Tongues, prophecy, knowledge, sacrifice — and the one thing without which they are nothing*

**Text:** 1 Corinthians 13:1–13 · **Supporting:** 1 Corinthians 13:2; 1 Corinthians 13:8; 1 Corinthians 13:12; 1 John 4:8

This is the most beautiful chapter in the New Testament, and it was written to the ugliest church in it. We read it at weddings. Paul wrote it to a congregation tearing itself apart over spiritual gifts. The setting matters, because it tells you what love is for — not a sentiment to decorate a marriage, but a verdict on a church that had everything except the one thing that counts.

**Without love, the gifts are zero**

Paul ends chapter 12 promising "a still more excellent way" (1 Corinthians 12:31), and then he lays it down with a series of subtractions that should have stopped the Corinthians cold. "If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels, but have not love, I am a noisy gong or a clanging cymbal. And if I have prophetic powers, and understand all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith, so as to remove mountains, but have not love, I am nothing" (1 Corinthians 13:1–2).

Read what he just emptied. The tongues they prized. The prophecy they ranked highest. The knowledge they were proud of. The faith that moves mountains. Every gift the Corinthians were competing over, Paul runs through the equation, and without love the answer is always the same number. Zero. Nothing. Noise.

He pushes it to the breaking point. "If I give away all I have, and if I deliver up my body to be burned, but have not love, I gain nothing" (1 Corinthians 13:3). You could die a martyr's death and gain nothing if love is not the engine. The Corinthians thought the impressive gift was the measure of the spiritual person. Paul says the gift can be total and the person still be nothing. Love is not one virtue among the gifts. It is the thing that makes any of them count.

Notice what this does to the Corinthian scoreboard. They had a ranking of believers based on the visibility of their gifts, and Paul takes the ranking and throws it out, because the measure was never the gift. A nobody with no platform and great love outweighs an apostle with every gift and none. This is the great equalizer of the church — the single woman praying alone, the old man who only knows how to be kind, the believer with no visible gift at all, can possess in full the one thing without which the most gifted preacher is noise. The currency of the kingdom is not ability. It is love, and it is available to everyone, which is exactly why it humbles the proud.

**What love actually does**

Then Paul refuses to leave love as a warm word and forces it into verbs — and every one of them indicts Corinth. "Love is patient and kind; love does not envy or boast; it is not arrogant or rude. It does not insist on its own way; it is not irritable or resentful; it does not rejoice at wrongdoing, but rejoices with the truth" (1 Corinthians 13:4–6).

Lay that beside the church it was written to. They were envious of each other's gifts — love does not envy. They were puffed up with knowledge — love is not arrogant. They insisted on their rights and their freedoms — love does not insist on its own way. They dragged each other to court and gloated — love is not resentful, does not rejoice at wrongdoing. Paul is not describing a feeling. He is describing the cross, and he is holding it up against the exact sins of the Corinthians, point for point. "Love bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things" (1 Corinthians 13:7).

**The one thing that never ends**

Then the reach into eternity. "Love never ends. As for prophecies, they will pass away; as for tongues, they will cease; as for knowledge, it will pass away" (1 Corinthians 13:8). The gifts the Corinthians were fighting over have an expiration date. They are scaffolding for a building under construction. "For we know in part and we prophesy in part, but when the perfect comes, the partial will pass away" (1 Corinthians 13:9–10). The day is coming when prophecy is unnecessary because the thing prophesied has arrived, when knowledge is swallowed by sight: "For now we see in a mirror dimly, but then face to face. Now I know in part; then I shall know fully, even as I have been fully known" (1 Corinthians 13:12).

When that day comes, the showy gifts will be obsolete. Love will not. "So now faith, hope, and love abide, these three; but the greatest of these is love" (1 Corinthians 13:13).

I cannot read this chapter without it reading me, because I have built ministry on the impressive thing and called it spiritual. I have prized the gift and starved the love. I have been right and unkind, knowledgeable and arrogant, capable and resentful, and Paul does the arithmetic on a man like that and writes nothing. The gifts I have been most proud of are the ones that will not survive the coming of Christ, and the love I have neglected is the only thing that will.

This is not poetry detached from the cross. It is the cross in prose. "God is love" (1 John 4:8), and we know what that love does because we watched it — patient, kind, bearing all things, not insisting on its own way, delivered up not to be admired but to be crucified. The crucified Christ is 1 Corinthians 13 in flesh and blood. He did not remove mountains to impress us. He went to a cross to love us. And the love that never ends is the love that hung there fully knowing us and chose us anyway.

So examine the thing you are most proud of, and run the equation Paul ran. Without love, what is it?

Without love you are nothing.

## Worship Aimed at the Other
*Why love ranks the clear word above the impressive one*

**Text:** 1 Corinthians 14:1–40 · **Supporting:** 1 Corinthians 14:12; 1 Corinthians 14:24–25; 1 Corinthians 14:40; 1 Corinthians 13:5

Tell a church love seeks the other's good, and the very next question is what that does to the way they gather. Paul does not leave it abstract. He takes the love of chapter 13 and pushes it straight into the worship service, and the result reorganizes everything the Corinthians were proud of in the room.

**Pursue love, and want the gift that builds others**

The bridge is explicit. "Pursue love, and earnestly desire the spiritual gifts, especially that you may prophesy" (1 Corinthians 14:1). Love comes first, and then it sorts the gifts — not by which is most impressive, but by which serves the people in the room. "The one who speaks in a tongue builds up himself, but the one who prophesies builds up the church" (1 Corinthians 14:4).

There is the ranking, and it is the opposite of Corinth's. They prized tongues because tongues looked spiritual, sounded heavenly, marked the speaker as advanced. Paul does not forbid them — he says, "Now I want you all to speak in tongues, but even more to prophesy" (1 Corinthians 14:5) — but he subordinates the showy gift to the clear one, because the clear one feeds the body and the showy one, untranslated, feeds only the self. "If the bugle gives an indistinct sound, who will get ready for battle?" (1 Corinthians 14:8). A word no one understands is a sound, not a sermon.

Then the principle that governs the whole chapter: "Since you are eager for manifestations of the Spirit, strive to excel in building up the church" (1 Corinthians 14:12). Want the gifts — but want them aimed at the other. The measure of a gift in the gathering is not how it makes you feel but how it builds the people beside you. That is love of chapter 13 — "it does not insist on its own way" (1 Corinthians 13:5) — walking into the worship service and rearranging the furniture.

This is why Paul can be so practical without being cold. The instructions about taking turns and interpreting and keeping order are not bureaucratic — they are love made specific. Love asks, before it speaks in the gathering, whether the person beside me will understand and be helped. Self-display asks only whether I will be noticed. The same gift can serve either master. A tongue interpreted feeds the church; a tongue paraded feeds the speaker. The difference is never the gift. The difference is whether love or self is holding it, and the gathered church is the place where that difference becomes visible to everyone.

This is the quiet exam every worship service runs on the people leading it. You cannot tell, from the gift alone, whose good a person is seeking. You can tell from the order, the patience, the willingness to translate, the readiness to fall silent so another can speak. Love is not loud about itself. It simply keeps building the people in the room, and lets the building be the proof.

**Worship that the outsider can understand**

Paul keeps the outsider in view, the seeker who wanders in. If everyone is speaking in tongues, "will they not say that you are out of your minds?" (1 Corinthians 14:23). But the clear, convicting word does something the impressive noise never could. "But if all prophesy, and an unbeliever or outsider enters, he is convicted by all, he is called to account by all, the secrets of his heart are disclosed, and so, falling on his face, he will worship God and declare that God is really among you" (1 Corinthians 14:24–25).

Read what intelligible worship accomplishes. The unbeliever is convicted. His heart is exposed. He falls on his face. He confesses that God is here. The Corinthians wanted worship that displayed their gifts; Paul wants worship that converts the stranger. A service arranged to impress the insider cannot do what a service arranged to reach the outsider does. Love builds the church and, in building it, opens the door for the one outside it.

**Order, because God is not confusion**

So Paul gives them practical structure — take turns, let one speak at a time, interpret what is said, weigh what is prophesied, keep it orderly (1 Corinthians 14:27–33). Not to quench the Spirit, but because of who the Spirit is. "For God is not a God of confusion but of peace" (1 Corinthians 14:33). The character of the worship should match the character of the God being worshiped. And he lands it: "But all things should be done decently and in order" (1 Corinthians 14:40).

Order is not the enemy of the Spirit. Chaos is not the evidence of His presence. A self-centered worship service that leaves everyone impressed and no one built up is not more spiritual for being loud. It is just Corinth, mistaking expression for edification.

I have to confess this is a temptation pastors carry as much as congregations do. I have planned services with one eye on whether the room would be impressed by us, and I know what it is to value the moving moment over the clear word that actually feeds the hungry person in the third row. We can dress self-display in the language of the Spirit and call our preferences worship, and I have done it. The question Paul keeps asking — did this build them up? — is the question I am most tempted to skip.

And underneath the whole chapter is the cross again, because this entire instinct — to bend even worship toward the other's good — is the mind of Christ. The crucified Christ did not come to display Himself. He came to build us up at the cost of His own body, and the firstfruits of His resurrection are the guarantee that the church He is building will stand. Worship that imitates Him aims outward — at the brother who needs feeding, at the stranger who needs convicting, at the God who is not confusion but peace.

So when you gather, ask the only question love asks of a gift: did it build them up?

In worship, build the church up.

## If Christ Has Not Been Raised
*The whole gospel staked on an empty tomb, and a labor that is never wasted*

**Text:** 1 Corinthians 15:1–58 · **Supporting:** 1 Corinthians 15:17; 1 Corinthians 15:20; 1 Corinthians 15:54–55; Isaiah 25:8

Everything Paul has written comes to this. The divisions, the lawsuits, the gifts, the love — all of it rests on one event in history, and if that event did not happen, the whole letter is the careful ordering of a corpse. Some in Corinth were saying there is no resurrection of the dead. Paul does not treat it as a minor disagreement. He treats it as the thread that, pulled, unravels Christianity entirely.

**The gospel he received, and the witnesses who saw**

Paul goes back to bedrock. "For I delivered to you as of first importance what I also received: that Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day in accordance with the Scriptures, and that he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve" (1 Corinthians 15:3–5). Then more witnesses — five hundred at once, most still alive and able to be questioned, then James, then all the apostles, then Paul himself, "as to one untimely born" (1 Corinthians 15:6–8). This is not a doctrine he invented. It is a report he received, backed by people you could go and ask.

That detail matters more than we let it. Paul does not appeal to an inner experience or a private conviction that cannot be checked. He names witnesses, most of them still breathing, and effectively invites the Corinthians to go cross-examine them. Christianity stakes itself on a public event in real history, not a feeling that works whether or not anything happened. That is the courage of it and the risk of it. If the witnesses lied or the body decayed, the whole structure falls and Paul says so himself. He does not protect the claim from the test. He builds the test into the claim.

**The dominoes that fall if the tomb was full**

Then Paul does the most ruthless thing a preacher can do with his own message. He takes it apart. "If there is no resurrection of the dead, then not even Christ has been raised. And if Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is in vain and your faith is in vain" (1 Corinthians 15:13–14). He keeps pulling the thread. "We are even found to be misrepresenting God… your faith is futile and you are still in your sins. Then those also who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished" (1 Corinthians 15:15–18).

Watch what falls. The preaching — empty. The faith — futile. The apostles — liars. Your sins — still on you. The dead you buried in hope — gone, perished, nothing. And then the verdict on a hope that ends at the grave: "If in Christ we have hope in this life only, we are of all people most to be pitied" (1 Corinthians 15:19). Paul will not let Christianity be a useful philosophy that works whether or not the tomb was empty. Take away the resurrection and you have not damaged the gospel. You have deleted it.

This is the steel under the comfort. The Christian faith is not a set of timeless values that survive the falsification of its central claim. It is a claim about a body in a tomb on a Sunday morning. If that body stayed dead, we should be pitied, and Paul says so to our faces.

**But in fact Christ has been raised**

Then the hinge, the two words the whole chapter has been straining toward. "But in fact Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep" (1 Corinthians 15:20). Firstfruits — the first sheaf of a harvest that guarantees the rest. His resurrection is not a single exception to the law of the grave. It is the beginning of the end of the grave. "For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive" (1 Corinthians 15:22).

And so the body — the thing Corinth despised, the thing they thought was disposable — is the very thing God means to raise. "It is sown perishable; it is raised imperishable… It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body" (1 Corinthians 15:42, 44). Death itself is on the clock: "The last enemy to be destroyed is death" (1 Corinthians 15:26). And Paul reaches back to Isaiah for the funeral of the grave: "Death is swallowed up in victory" (1 Corinthians 15:54; Isaiah 25:8). Then he taunts it. "O death, where is your victory? O death, where is your sting?" (1 Corinthians 15:55).

I need this with a desperation I do not always admit. I have stood at gravesides — held the hands of widows, buried people I loved, looked at a small casket I will never forget — and I have nothing to say there if the tomb was full. Pastoral comfort is cruelty if the resurrection is a metaphor. But Christ has been raised, the firstfruits, and that turns the cemetery from an ending into a planting. The crucified Christ who died for our sins is the risen Christ who broke the grave open ahead of us. The cross paid for the sin; the empty tomb defeated the death the sin earned. Both, or neither.

**So your labor is not wasted**

Paul could have ended at the trumpet, but he brings the towering doctrine down to a Tuesday. "Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing that in the Lord your labor is not in vain" (1 Corinthians 15:58). Because the dead are raised, nothing done for Christ disappears into the ground. The faithfulness no one noticed, the prayer no one heard, the obedience that cost you and changed nothing visible — none of it is lost. The resurrection is the guarantee that the work is kept.

So work, beloved. Not because it pays now. Because the grave gave Him back, and it will give you back too.

Your labor is not in vain.

## The Collection, the Coming, and the Love
*How resurrection hope lands in an offering, a longing, and a charge to love*

**Text:** 1 Corinthians 16:1–24 · **Supporting:** 1 Corinthians 16:2; 1 Corinthians 16:13–14; 1 Corinthians 16:22; 1 Corinthians 15:58

Great doctrine always has to land somewhere ordinary, or it was never believed. Paul has just spent a chapter on the resurrection of the dead, the trumpet, the imperishable body, death swallowed up. And the very next word is about money. "Now concerning the collection" (1 Corinthians 16:1). The connection is not a letdown. It is the proof. A church that truly believes the dead will rise gives differently on Sunday morning.

**The resurrection turns into an offering**

The first thing Paul does with the towering hope of chapter 15 is organize a relief fund for the poor saints in Jerusalem. "On the first day of every week, each of you is to put something aside and store it up, as he may prosper" (1 Corinthians 16:2). Regular. Planned. Proportional. Every believer, every week, setting aside what God enabled — so that no frantic last-minute appeal would be needed when Paul arrived (1 Corinthians 16:2–3).

This is what "your labor is not in vain" (1 Corinthians 15:58) looks like by Monday. A people convinced their bodies will be raised do not clutch their money as if this life were all there is. The resurrection loosens the grip. The same Corinthians who had been fighting over rights and gifts are pointed outward, toward suffering brothers they would never meet, with a steady generosity that asks nothing in return. Eternity changes the budget. It always does.

This is the test of every doctrine we say we believe — what does it do to the ordinary week? A resurrection that changes nothing about how you handle your money on the first day of the week is a resurrection you have admired but not believed. Paul will not let the Corinthians treat chapter 15 as a thrilling idea to debate. He turns it immediately into an offering, a schedule, a habit, a brother in Jerusalem he will never meet being fed by a church a thousand miles away. The empty tomb has consequences in the checkbook, or it has not yet reached the heart.

And the workers Paul honors prove the same point from the other side. The household of Stephanas, devoted to the service of the saints, were not famous. They were faithful. In a letter that began with a church idolizing its celebrity teachers, Paul ends by commending the unglamorous servants who simply showed up and labored in love. The resurrection does not produce stars. It produces servants, because it tells them their hidden labor will be raised along with their bodies.

So the letter that opened by tearing down a church's pride closes by lifting up its servants and longing for its Lord. The corrections were never the point. Love was the point, all the way through, because love is what the cross looked like and love is what the empty tomb sends us back into the week to do.

**The longing that ends the letter**

Paul threads the chapter with his travel plans — Macedonia, Ephesus, a wintering with them perhaps (1 Corinthians 16:5–9) — and commends the workers: Timothy, Apollos, the household of Stephanas who "have devoted themselves to the service of the saints" (1 Corinthians 16:15). These are the field hands again, the servants, honored not for their platform but for their labor. And then, near the end of a hard letter full of correction, Paul lets a single Aramaic word escape that tells you what his heart was set on the whole time: "Maranatha" — "Our Lord, come" (1 Corinthians 16:22).

That is the longing under everything. Come, Lord. The church that will one day see Him face to face aches for the day. Paul does not end a letter of rebuke with bitterness. He ends it leaning toward the coming of Christ, the very Christ whose resurrection he has just proven, the firstfruits who will return for the harvest.

**Be watchful, be strong, and let love govern it all**

Then the charge, stacked like a soldier's orders. "Be watchful, stand firm in the faith, act like men, be strong" (1 Corinthians 16:13). Watchful, because the Lord is coming. Firm, because the resurrection is sure. Strong, because the labor is not wasted. And then the line that gathers the whole letter into one command and lands it: "Let all that you do be done in love" (1 Corinthians 16:14).

All that you do. The collection — in love. The watchfulness — in love. The standing firm, the correcting, the worship, the use of gifts, the surrender of rights, the discerning of the body at the table — all of it, in love. Paul has spent sixteen chapters dismantling a church's pride and division, and he hands them, at the end, the single thread that should run through every part of it. Not knowledge. Not gifts. Not even doctrine, as precious as the resurrection is. Love is the governing law of the redeemed life, because love is what we saw at the cross.

I cannot close this letter without confessing how often I have done good things without that thread running through them. I have corrected without love and called it faithfulness. I have served without love and called it commitment. I have given, and led, and even preached, with everything in place except the one thing the apostle says must be in everything. A church can get the doctrine of the resurrection exactly right and still do all of it loveless, and I have been that man more days than I want to count.

But the Lord we are told to long for is the crucified and risen Christ — the One who loved us to the cross and out of the tomb, the firstfruits who guarantees our raising. "Maranatha." Come, Lord. And until He comes, the shape of the waiting is love, because love is the shape of the One we are waiting for. The whole letter — every fracture healed, every right surrendered, every body discerned, every grave defeated — comes to rest here, in the simplest command Paul ever gave them.

Let all you do be love.
